extracted.intended_audience: readers and scholars interested in biblical textual criticism and Hebrew numeral translation (Old Testament revisers, philologists)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical standards for translating and interpreting Hebrew numeric expressions in Biblical texts, with emphasis on syntactic order, use of conjunctions, grammatical number, and internal consistency of ages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hebrew concrete-number ordering (claimed larger-first rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: "In reading concrete numbers, the Hebrews gave the larger number first."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This claim is contestable and not universally true; the page gives counterexamples (e.g., Genesis xiv.14; Genesis v.3) where the larger number is placed last. Do not assume a single fixed ordering rule without checking individual instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not insert conjunctions not present in the Hebrew
rubrics_metrics.description: "The real question... is whether... putting in a conjunction where there is none in the Hebrew is justifiable."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translators should not add an 'and' (or other words) where the Hebrew text omits it unless there is clear grammatical or contextual justification; adding conjunctions can produce artificial readings that conflict with the text's grammar and internal numeric relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect grammatical number (pluralization) in translation
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that the word 'hundred' may appear in the plural (e.g., yielding literally 'nine hundreds year, and thirty year').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translations and reinterpretations must account for plural forms and their syntactic consequences; an explanatory theory must reconcile plural morphology with the proposed numeric reading rather than ignoring it as inconvenient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain internal arithmetic consistency (ages must add up)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ages given before and after the birth of a son should add together to equal the stated whole age; any translation method that breaks this additive relation is incorrect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the internal numerical relations in the narrative (e.g., 'X years and then Y years after begetting Z, total = X+Y') as a consistency test for any proposed alternate rendering. The page demonstrates that a proposed inversion method yields contradictions (e.g., impossible totals for Adam, Seth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assert absence of Hebrew numeric forms without evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: "Mr. Bryant says... the Hebrews had no means of writing 'nine hundred,' or any number of hundreds above one, without repetition or circumlocution.' This is an assertion without proof."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that certain numeric expressions were impossible or unwritable in biblical Hebrew must be supported by grammatical or epigraphic evidence; the page cites known Hebrew lexical forms for hundreds (ma-ah = 100; mathayim = 200; sh'loth ma-oth = 300, etc.) to rebut unsupported claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize historical variation in unit/tens ordering
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Hebrew grammar (see Conant's 'Gesenius', for instance) teaches that 'when units and tens are written together, the early writers commonly place the units first, as 'two and twenty'; the later writers almost invariably reversing them, as 'twenty and two.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply knowledge of diachronic/historical variation: patterns that hold for units and tens in different strata of Hebrew cannot be naively extrapolated to hundreds/thousands. Translation rules should be sensitive to authorial period and usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use presence/absence of conjunctions to guide literal rendering
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: 'in Genesis v.3 the Hebrew has a conjunction between the two numerals, reading "thirty and a hundred," so that the most literal translation gives one hundred and thirty'; in verse 4 'eight hundred years' appears 'with no and (u or v) between eight and a hundred.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a conjunction is present between numerals, prefer literal rendering that reflects that conjunction; when it is absent, do not force a conjunction into translation. Let the textual detail (presence/absence of u/v) determine the literal phrasing unless strong reason exists otherwise.
